Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Kaikea's memories of that fateful night still feel like a living thing, suffocating him with every recall. It was five years ago, when he was pulled over by police for a routine traffic stop. What should have been a mundane encounter turned into a nightmare as the officer became increasingly aggressive, eventually drawing his gun and ordering Kaikea out of the car. The sound of the officer's voice, the metallic click of the gun, still echoes in Kaikea's mind like it happened yesterday. The memory is so extreme that it's hard for him to believe it actually happened – "did I really see what I think I saw?" he often wonders. Yet, every time he recalls that night, the terror comes flooding back, as if no time has passed at all. It's not just the memory itself, but also the thoughts and emotions that come with it. When Kaikea remembers the event, he starts to feel like something is off, like the world around him is not quite right. He becomes hyper-vigilant, expecting something bad to happen at any moment. Even ordinary sounds – a car horn honking, someone dropping a bag – make him jump or startle. It's these triggers that have become a constant companion for Kaikea. Physical proximity to others makes him feel uneasy, like he's trapped and can't escape. Driving with people in the car is even worse – every sudden movement, every unexpected noise, sends his heart racing. And then there are the somatic symptoms: feeling nauseous when he thinks about that night or encounters a trigger. It's as if his body is trying to tell him something, warning him of an impending threat. Kaikea has come to believe that these triggers are warnings signs, indications that something bad is lurking just around the corner. When something takes longer than expected – like a delayed flight or a traffic jam – he assumes the worst: "something's gone wrong," "there's been an accident." Even strangers approaching him in ordinary situations make him feel threatened, like they might be hiding something. As Kaikea navigates his daily life as an airline pilot, these triggers and threats are always present. He avoids flying with certain crew members or taking routes that remind him of that night. His colleagues have started to notice the changes in him – he's more withdrawn, less confident. But for Kaikea, it's all about survival: "if I can just avoid X, Y, Z, I'll be safe." The problem is, these avoidance behaviors only seem to reinforce his fears, making him feel like he's constantly on edge. It's this perpetual state of threat and vigilance that has brought Kaikea to seek help. He's exhausted from living in a world where every sound, every movement, every delay feels like a potential danger sign. What he hopes for most is to break free from this cycle of fear and start rebuilding his life – one where memories don't feel more real than reality itself.
